title: Perspectives on the Indian National Movement

scenes.text: Was India's freedom struggle a united national movement or divided elite politics?
scenes.narration: Imagine looking at one historical event through four completely different pairs of glasses. That is how scholars debate the Indian National Movement.

scenes.text: Cricket commentators arguing whether a team played for shared pride or personal gain.
scenes.narration: Think of this as an analogy: when your school cricket team wins, some celebrate pure unity, while critics say players only chased personal glory. That same debate divides our historians.

scenes.heading: Imperialist vs Nationalist Views
scenes.narration: Here is the clash. Imperialist administrators like Lord Curzon dismissed India as merely a geographical expression led by power brokers. Early nationalists countered that India was a nation in the making.

scenes.heading: Cultural Nationalists vs Marxists
scenes.narration: Aurobindo Ghosh argued India was a nation from the beginning. But Marxist thinkers viewed nationalism as an invented tradition serving the bourgeoisie, meaning the wealthy capitalist class.

scenes.name: B.R. Ambedkar
scenes.idea: Demanded social fraternity and criticized Congress, arguing caste oppression must end first.
scenes.narration: From the Dalit and subaltern perspective, which focuses on marginalized groups, Ambedkar rejected Congress. He argued true nationhood requires social fraternity, not just replacing the British while caste oppression remains.

scenes.heading: Socialist and Radical Humanist Views
items: Nehru and Bose introduced socialist ideas into Congress
M.N. Roy argued nationalism suppresses individual freedom
scenes.narration: Inside Congress, socialists like Nehru and the Congress Socialist Party worked to radicalize programmes for workers. In contrast, M.N. Roy argued nationalism suppresses man, urging a cosmopolitan union of liberated individuals.

items: Imperialists saw power brokers, but nationalists asserted growing unity.
Marxists exposed bourgeois interests behind the national movement.
Dalit and subaltern thinkers demanded social equality and fraternity.
scenes.narration: Here is your recap: imperialists questioned unity, nationalists defended it, while Marxists and subaltern thinkers highlighted class and caste inequalities. Remember these lenses, and PSIR becomes simple!
